supplement

supplement helps you share the supplemental materials of a research paper as a website: analysis reports, code, and open data. Each report is a page of one Quarto site, so every page has the site navigation. Quarto stores each report’s computed output in _freeze/. So once each report holds stored output, the site rebuilds without the data. GitHub Pages serves the site, and Zenodo’s GitHub integration can archive each GitHub release with a DOI.

The package is in early development.

Start a new site

The guide Publish a supplement site is for your first site. It goes step by step from an empty folder to a site on GitHub Pages with a Zenodo DOI. In R, vignette("publishing", package = "supplement") opens it when the package was installed with its vignettes.

You need the Quarto command-line interface, and R with the knitr and rmarkdown packages, to render the site. You can make the site folder from R or from Quarto. In R, supplement::check_tools() reports which of these tools are missing, too old, or not on the system path. It also checks for git and the GitHub CLI (gh).

From R, install the package from GitHub with pak::pak("jmgirard/supplement"). Then run:

supplement::create_supplement("my-supplement", repo = "owner/name")

The first argument is the folder for the site. It can be a new folder or a clone of a new GitHub repository. repo is the GitHub repository, which the function writes into the site’s GitHub links. You can leave it out and edit the OWNER and REPO placeholders in _quarto.yml and _README.md yourself. If the folder already holds a file that the template writes, the function stops and writes nothing.

From Quarto, in a new, empty folder or in a clone of a new GitHub repository, run:

quarto use template jmgirard/supplement/inst/template

Quarto asks whether to put the site in a new subdirectory. In a folder that is not empty, such as a clone, the default answer is yes, so type n. GitHub Pages serves docs/ only at the top of the repository.

With either route, render the site once in its folder before your first commit:

quarto render

The first render writes .gitignore and README.md, a short page for the people who read the site’s repository. If the folder already has a README.md, the render keeps it and removes _README.md. ?create_supplement explains how the first render sets up these files. The guide for the site’s authors is GUIDE.md. It explains how the site renders, how to render on the machine that holds private data, and how to publish. It also shows how to record R packages with renv and how to render reports in a Docker container.

Put the paper title, citation, Zenodo DOIs, and data files in _supplement.yml. The home page reads them from that file. GUIDE.md lists the values and describes the shortcodes that show them.

Add reports and data

In R, run these functions in the site folder:

supplement::add_report("models", "Model Comparison", "Fits and compares the models.")
supplement::add_data("path/to/scores.csv", "Scores of each participant")

add_report() writes analyses/models.qmd, with the title and the description in its front matter. The report ends with a “Computing environment” section that shows the R and package versions of its last render. The function also adds a link to the report to the Analyses menu in _quarto.yml. The home page lists each report in analyses/ with its title and description.

add_data() copies the file into data/ and adds it to the data list in _supplement.yml. If the file is directly in data/, the function does not copy it. The data table on the home page lists each file in that list. Every file in data/ is published on the site.

?add_report describes how the function edits _quarto.yml, and ?add_data how it edits _supplement.yml. Each page also describes the error for a missing menu or list.

Record the R setup

To record the version of each R package that the reports use, so that another machine can install the same versions, use the renv package. The “Recording R packages with renv” part of GUIDE.md shows the three commands. supplement does not call renv.

In R, supplement::write_dockerfile(quarto = "1.10.19") in the site folder reads renv.lock and writes a Dockerfile and a .dockerignore. Docker builds an image from them. The image holds the R version and the R packages in renv.lock, and Quarto. A report can render in it where Docker runs Linux containers on amd64, or on arm64 for R 4.1.0 or later. The “Running reports in a container” part of GUIDE.md shows how to build the image and render a report in it.

Check a site before a release

In R, run this function in the site folder:

supplement::check_supplement()

check_supplement() changes no file. It prints each problem that it finds and returns the problems as a data frame, with one row per problem. ?check_supplement describes each check and its limits, for example the links that it does not test. It finds:

  • files larger than GitHub’s limit of 100 MiB
  • saved R objects, such as .rds files, that git tracks or does not ignore
  • files in figures/, docs/, and _freeze/ that git ignores, which a release leaves out
  • reports directly in analyses/ with code and no stored output in _freeze/
  • reports directly in analyses/ whose stored output in _freeze/ came from other text than the report holds now, or whose source hash cannot be read
  • reports directly in analyses/ whose stored output gives another MD5 of _scripts/report.R than the file has now
  • folders in _freeze/analyses/ that no file or folder in analyses/ names, as after a report is deleted or renamed
  • reports directly in analyses/ that name a missing _scripts/report.R file
  • a site with no docs/ folder
  • relative href, src, and xlink:href links in docs/ to files that are not in docs/, or to folders there with no index.html
  • symbolic links in docs/ to existing files or folders outside docs/, and on Windows junctions to folders outside docs/
  • pages in docs/ that cannot be read
  • figures in figures/ whose copy in docs/figures/ is missing or differs
  • DOIs in CITATION.cff or on the home page that differ from _supplement.yml, and a CITATION.cff that cannot be read
  • template placeholders left in place, such as the paper title in _supplement.yml or the unchanged example report

Make a release

_supplement.yml holds the site version under supplement:, for example version: "1.0.0". A new site has version: "" until its first release. write_citation() and write_zenodo() write the version to CITATION.cff and .zenodo.json.

In R, run this function in the site folder:

supplement::release_supplement("major")

release_supplement() takes "patch", "minor", "major", or a version such as "1.0.0". A word raises that part of the version and sets the parts after it to 0. An empty version counts as 0.0.0, so "major" gives 1.0.0. A version must be greater than the current version.

Before it changes any file, the function runs check_supplement(). If that finds a problem, the function stops and changes no file. If check_supplement() cannot run git, for example in a folder that is not in a git repository, the function also stops. A DOI in CITATION.cff that differs from _supplement.yml does not stop it, because the release writes that file again. Then it changes the version in _supplement.yml and writes CITATION.cff and .zenodo.json again.

Last, the function prints the commands that make the release, for example:

git status -- .
git add -A -- .
git commit -m "Release v1.0.0" -- .
git tag v1.0.0
git push
git push origin v1.0.0
gh release create v1.0.0 --generate-notes

It runs none of them. Read them, then run them yourself in the site folder. The last command needs the GitHub command-line tool, gh. After Zenodo archives the release, add the new version DOI to _supplement.yml and render the site again. ?release_supplement describes the cases that stop the function and how it puts back the files after a failed write. It also explains the -- . in the git commands.
